Everything here is built on this device. Nothing you write is sent anywhere.
What this app keeps, and what it never sends

Your projects, your keys and your packages stay in this app’s own storage on this device. Nothing you write is uploaded, and the app opens no connection of its own. A link you tap is handed to whichever app you choose to open it with.
What you may do with what this builds

What you build here is yours. The app is given as it is, with no promise that a package it produces suits any purpose of yours. Signing keys are yours to keep safe: nobody, this app included, can recover one you lose.
Your ideas, suggestions and problems matter to us.

What do you want help with?
Everything you want to know about Omni Builder is here. Learn quickly, discover more.
What this app is, and where to begin

Omni Builder compiles Android packages on this device. There is no server and no desktop toolchain: the compiler, the packager and the signer all run here. Make a project from Home, write your code under Java, then build it.

A project needs a name, a package name such as com.example.app, a version, and the Android versions it runs on. The package name is what Android knows an installed app by, so choose it before you publish rather than after. An icon can be added at any time from Files.
The editor, and what it checks as you type

Files opens a project. Tapping a source file opens the editor, which colours the code and checks it a moment after you stop typing. Names it already knows are offered as you type, and it will jump to where a name was written or list everywhere it is used.
From sources to an APK and a bundle

Build compiles the sources, packs the resources, writes the dex, seals the package and then verifies what it wrote. It produces an APK to install here and a bundle to upload. Every build needs a signing key, and a shared one is made for you the first time.
Keys, passwords, and what a signature proves

Every package is signed. A signature proves the package came from the key that signed it, and Android refuses an update signed by a different key. Keep your key and its password somewhere safe: a lost key cannot be replaced, and the app it signed can never be updated again.
Reading a refusal, and fixing what it names

A refusal names a code, the file and the line it is about, and says what it wants instead. Project health lists what is wrong with a project before a build starts. Where the repair is one this app can make itself, it offers it and shows what it would change first.
The refusal codes are documented inside the app itself. Every code an editor check or a build raises carries a sentence, in the language you chose, saying what it means and what to do about it.
If none of this answers it, write to us. Say what you did, what you expected, and what happened instead.

The questions asked most, and their answers.

This app was made for Android itself. Gradle and the desktop tools were not written for a phone and are not fully supported there. So this carries its own build engine and no outside dependency, which makes building faster, steadier and at home on a phone.
Why is the app this small?
There are hundreds of megabytes between this and the tools it stands beside. A compiler written for the job, and a package holding only what is needed, is the whole of the difference.
Which sites can Web To Apk wrap?
Any site that loads in a browser. The address is opened in a WebView inside your own package, so what the site can do there is what it can do in a browser.
Can a project be moved or deleted?
Yes. A project is a plain folder: move it, copy it, back it up or delete it with any file manager. Deleting one from here sends it to the trash, where it waits a day.

This uses the Wireless debugging that Android 11 and later carry. If the option is not on your device, check its software version.
This connects the phone to a computer over USB. The steps are the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Settings › About phone › Software information. Tap the build number seven times to turn developer options on.
Settings › Developer options › Wireless debugging. Turn it on, then tap Pair device with pairing code.
A notification asks for the pairing code. Open the panel and type the six digits shown on the other screen.
Download the Android SDK Platform Tools from the official page and unpack them somewhere on the computer.
On the phone, Settings › About phone › Software information, tap the build number seven times, then turn USB debugging on under developer options.
Plug the phone in with a cable that carries data, open a terminal in the platform-tools folder and run adb devices.
